config.title: Diameter of Binary Tree

intro.title: Diameter of Binary Tree
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function to find the diameter of a binary tree, which is the length of the longest path between any two nodes in the tree. You will learn to traverse the tree using depth-first search (DFS) to calculate heights and track the maximum diameter. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, recursion, and basic tree node structures. This exercise will help you understand tree properties and improve your lesson-solving skills with recursive algorithms.
intro.usecase: The diameter of a binary tree algorithm is essential in network routing systems where you need to find the longest path between any two nodes to optimize data transmission. In file system structures, it helps determine the maximum depth between directories for efficient storage organization and access patterns. Game developers use this concept to calculate the farthest distance between game objects in hierarchical scene graphs for collision detection and AI pathfinding. Database systems apply similar tree traversal patterns to optimize query execution plans across hierarchical data relationships.

objectives: Construct a binary tree node class with left and right child references
Implement a recursive depth-first search function to traverse the binary tree
Initialize variables to track both node height and maximum diameter during traversal
Manipulate the traversal function to calculate height while updating the diameter
Apply the algorithm to compute the diameter for various binary tree structures
Integrate the diameter calculation into a complete solution function
Control the base case conditions to handle empty tree scenarios

content.body: The longest path between any two nodes in a tree is called its diameter. Finding this distance requires exploring branches carefully. Let's learn how to calculate the diameter of a binary tree efficiently.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
• Apply depth-first thinking to explore tree branches
• Implement a recursive function that tracks heights
• Explain why the diameter might not pass through the root
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Look at this small tree. The diameter is the longest path between any two nodes. Which two nodes are farthest apart? (Count edges between them.)
content.title: Try it
content.visualMetaphor: Show exploring from the root down branches; one level or one branch at a time.

content.body: You visually traced paths through the tree, exploring different branches from the root outward. This manual checking works for small trees.
content.title: What you did

content.body: With larger trees, manually checking every possible path becomes overwhelming. We need a systematic way to explore branches without missing the longest path.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Trees are explored from the root down branches. At each node, we need to know: how deep are its left and right branches? The longest path through this node would combine those depths. We'll visit nodes one at a time, keeping track of heights as we go.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Use branch/root visual reasoning; visiting nodes or exploring levels one at a time.

content.body: We'll use depth-first traversal. For each node, calculate the height of its left and right subtrees. The diameter at that node is left height + right height. Track the maximum diameter found anywhere in the tree. The base case: an empty tree has height 0.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Start from the root, traverse depth-first
2. For each node, if it's null, return height 0
3. Recursively get heights of left and right subtrees
4. Update global diameter with left + right heights
5. Return height of current node (1 + max(left, right))
6. After traversal, return the maximum diameter found

content.body: You've implemented an efficient O(n) solution! Remember: the diameter is the maximum of (left height + right height) at any node. We explore branches depth-first, combining heights as we go. The base case of an empty tree (height 0) ensures our recursion stops properly.
